blocks.content: While a court of law is bound by the strict rules of evidence and procedure, a tribunal is guided by the principles of natural justice.

rows: Strictly bound by Evidence Act and CPC/CrPC
Guided by Principles of Natural Justice
Limited strictly to specified statutory matters
Possesses inherent powers under civil law
Lacks inherent powers; limited to statutory provisions

items: Article 323A tribunals can ONLY be created by Parliament; state legislatures have no power under 323A.

L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997): Appeals against Tribunal decisions must first go to the Division Bench of the concerned High Court, as judicial review under Article 226/227 is a basic feature of the Constitution.
Swaran Singh Committee recommended the insertion of Part XIV-A (Tribunals) into the Constitution.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Courts are part of the traditional judicial system established to administer justice according to strict legal procedures.
Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies created under Part XIV-A of the Constitution for speedy disposal of administrative and specialized disputes.
Courts are bound strictly by the Indian Evidence Act and the Code of Civil Procedure, whereas Tribunals follow the Principles of Natural Justice.
Article 323A empowers ONLY Parliament to establish Administrative Tribunals, whereas Article 323B allows both Parliament and State Legislatures to set up tribunals for specific matters.
Courts are presided over solely by judicial officers, while Tribunals consist of both judicial and technical/administrative members.
